title: Cards and colours
objectives: Solve card puzzles by conditioning on the right event.

screens.title: Cards and colours
screens.prose:
This level conditions. The same books, easiest first:

- Mosteller, *Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability*: cards, urns, duels
- Zhou, the green book: Bayes, ruin, order statistics
- Crack, *Heard on the Street*: fast conditioning questions
- Joshi and co-authors: harder ruin and maxima
- *Probability and Markets*, a free guide from a trading firm: conditioning as pricing

screens.title: Red, then red?
screens.prose: Six cards: three red, three black. The first card dealt is the 4♥. The second card comes from the five still in the deck.

state.caption: Six cards, three red and three black. The first card dealt was the 4♥.

screens.question: Tap every card that would make the second card red.

hints.text: Only cards still in the deck can come second.
The 4♥ has already gone.
Two red cards are left: the 9♦ and the Q♥.

feedback.correct: Two of the five cards left are red, so the chance is $\tfrac25$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap only red cards that are still in the deck.

byKey.kept: You tapped the 4♥ too. It is already dealt, so it cannot be the second card.

explain.text: Knowing the first card is red removes it. The second card is one of five, two of them red. So the chance is $\tfrac25$, not $\tfrac36$.

screens.title: A full deck
screens.prose: Now a full deck. The first card is red. We **condition** on that: remove it and count what is left.

state.caption: A full deck after one red card has gone.

screens.question: What is the chance the second card is red? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: How many cards are left, and how many of them are red?
25 red cards remain among 51.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the red cards left over the cards left.

byKey.half: You ignored the first card. One red card has gone, so red is now slightly less likely.
byKey.kept: You kept 26 red cards. One of them is the card already dealt.
byKey.den: You took one red card away but left 52 cards in the deck.

explain.text: After one red card, 25 of the 51 cards left are red. The chance is $25/51 \approx 0.4902$. The condition shrinks both the count and the deck.

screens.title: The second card, unseen
screens.prose: Shuffle a full deck and deal five cards face down. Nobody looks at any of them.

state.caption: Nobody has looked at any card. The second one is ringed.

screens.question: What is the chance the second card is an ace? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: You know nothing about the first card.
With no information, is the second place any different from the first?
Every position holds each card with chance $\tfrac1{52}$, so an ace with chance $\tfrac4{52}$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac4{52} = \tfrac1{13} \approx 0.0769$, the same as for the top card.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Nobody saw the first card, so nothing has been removed.

byKey.fifty-one: You used 4 aces in 51 cards. That conditions on the first card not being an ace, which nobody knows.
byKey.three: You assumed the first card was an ace. Nobody has seen it.

explain.text: Every ordering of the deck is equally likely, so every position is alike. The second card is an ace with chance $\tfrac{4}{52} = \tfrac1{13}$. This is **symmetry of positions**: unseen cards change nothing.

screens.title: Where is the first ace?
screens.prose: Turn a shuffled deck over one card at a time. The four aces cut the 48 other cards into five gaps.

state.caption: One shuffle: the four aces at positions 8, 19, 33 and 47.

screens.question: On average, at what position does the first ace appear? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: The five gaps are alike by symmetry.
Each gap holds $48/5 = 9.6$ cards on average.
The first ace comes after gap 1: $9.6 + 1 = 10.6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Share the 48 other cards among five gaps, then add the ace itself.

byKey.thirteen: You split 52 cards into four parts. Four aces make five gaps, not four.
byKey.quarter: You used four gaps. The aces make five: before, between and after them.
byKey.no-ace: That is the cards before the first ace. Add one for the ace itself.

explain.text: Four aces cut the others into five gaps, alike by symmetry. Gap 1 holds $48/5 = 9.6$ cards on average. The first ace is next, at $10.6$.

screens.title: The card after the first ace
screens.prose: Turn cards over until the first ace appears. Then turn one more card.

state.caption: The A♥ is the first ace. What comes next?

screens.question: What is the chance that this next card is the ace of spades?

options.text: Less than $\tfrac1{52}$, as the A♠ is itself the first ace a quarter of the time
options.why: That is the answer most people blurt. Put the A♠ just after the first ace of the other 51 cards. Each such deck matches one 51-card order: a share $51!/52!$.

options.text: $\tfrac1{51}$, one of the 51 cards not yet the first ace
options.why: You spread the chance over 51 cards. Which card is first changes from deck to deck, so each of the 52 cards gets exactly $\tfrac1{52}$.

options.text: $\tfrac14$, as one of the four aces is next
options.why: You treated the next card as an ace for sure. Most of the time it is one of the 48 other cards.

hints.text: Count the decks where the A♠ sits right after the first ace.
Take out the A♠ and shuffle the other 51 cards.
Put the A♠ back just after their first ace. Each 51-card order gives one such deck: $51!/52! = \tfrac1{52}$.

feedback.correct: Exactly $\tfrac1{52}$, the same as for any named card.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count decks with the A♠ just after the first ace by building them.

byKey.b: You worried the A♠ might be the first ace. Build the decks instead: put it just after the first ace of the other 51. That gives $51!$ decks, a share $\tfrac1{52}$.

explain.text: Remove the A♠, shuffle the other 51, and slot it in just after their first ace. That is a one-to-one match with the $51!$ orders, so the chance is $51!/52! = \tfrac1{52}$. The same swap works for the 2♣, or any card.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose:
Two moves solved every card puzzle. **Condition**: remove what you know and count what is left. **Symmetry**: unseen positions are alike, and $k$ special cards cut $n - k$ others into $k + 1$ gaps.

$$E[\text{position of the first special card}] = \frac{n + 1}{k + 1}$$
screens.question: A shuffled deck, nothing seen. What is the chance the 30th card is red?

options.text: It depends on the first 29 cards
options.why: Nobody has seen the first 29. With no information every position is alike.
You removed a card nobody has seen. Nothing is known, so nothing is removed.

hints.text: What do you know about the first 29 cards?
Nothing has been seen.
Every position is alike: $26/52$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{26}{52} = \tfrac12$: the 30th place is like the first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Nothing is known, so use symmetry.

explain.text: With nothing seen, the 30th card is as likely to be any card as the top one. So it is red with chance $\tfrac12$.

screens.title: The gap argument
screens.prose: We found the first ace at $10.6$ on average. Now put the argument in order, as you would say it.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Pick any one of the 48 non-aces and look at it with the four aces.
Its place among those five cards is equally likely to be any of five. So it beats every ace with chance $\tfrac15$.
Add these indicators by linearity: $48 \times \tfrac15 = 9.6$ non-aces come before the first ace on average.
The first ace comes straight after them, at $9.6 + 1 = 10.6$.
The aces split the deck into four equal parts, so the first ace is at 13.

hints.text: Start from one non-ace card.
Its chance of beating all four aces is $\tfrac15$.
One card, its chance, linearity, then add the ace.

feedback.correct: One card, its chance of coming first, linearity, then the ace itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with a single non-ace and its chance of coming before every ace.

byKey.d1: Four aces make five gaps, not four parts. That line gives 13, which is too late.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the one about four parts belongs.
byKey.s4: The ace is added last, once the count before it is known.

explain.text: Each non-ace beats all four aces with chance $\tfrac15$, so $48/5$ of them come first on average. Linearity needs no independence. The first ace is then at $53/5 = 10.6$.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three new puzzles. Allow about 3 minutes each, 9 in all, as an interview would. Keep your own time. Give each answer to four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

rows: Two cards are dealt. What is the chance they share a suit?
Two cards are dealt. What is the chance of at least one ace?
A full deck is turned over. How many red cards do you expect before the first black one?

hints.text: Condition on the first card in the first two. Use gaps in the third.
After any first card, 12 of the 51 left share its suit.
$\tfrac{12}{51}$; $1 - \tfrac{48}{52}\cdot\tfrac{47}{51}$; the 26 blacks make 27 gaps for the reds, so $\tfrac{26}{27}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Check the first answer. The first card is gone, so 12 of the 51 left share its suit.
byKey.r1c1: Check the second answer. Adding $\tfrac4{52}$ twice counts two aces twice; use $1 - P(\text{no ace})$.
byKey.r2c1: Check the third answer. The 26 black cards make 27 gaps, not 26.

explain.text: Same suit: $12/51 \approx 0.2353$. At least one ace: $1 - (48 \cdot 47)/(52 \cdot 51) = 33/221 \approx 0.1493$. Reds before the first black: 26 reds over 27 gaps, $26/27 \approx 0.9630$.

screens.title: Follow-up: the first heart
screens.prose: You answered 10.6 for the first ace. The interviewer asks at once: and the first heart?
screens.question: On average, at what position does the first heart appear? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Now there are 13 special cards.
They cut the 39 others into 14 gaps.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $(n + 1)/(k + 1)$ with 13 hearts.

byKey.four: You split 52 into 13 parts. Thirteen hearts make 14 gaps.
byKey.thirteen-gaps: You used 13 gaps. Thirteen hearts make 14.
byKey.no-card: That is the cards before the first heart. Add one for the heart.

explain.text: Thirteen hearts cut 39 other cards into 14 gaps of $39/14$ on average. The first heart is next: $53/14 \approx 3.79$. Saying the general formula, $(n + 1)/(k + 1)$, shows the interviewer you can take any $k$.

screens.title: Two losing days
screens.prose: A month of P&L has 21 trading days, 8 of them losing. A risk manager picks two different days at random to review.

state.caption: Daily P&L in £k over 21 trading days. The 8 losing days are shaded.

screens.question: What is the chance both days are losing days? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Condition on the first day being a losing day.
Then 7 of the 20 days left are losing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The second day is picked from the 20 days left.

byKey.replace: You squared $\tfrac8{21}$. The same day cannot be picked twice, so the second chance is $\tfrac7{20}$.
byKey.one: That is the chance for one day. Both must be losing days.

explain.text: The first pick is a losing day with chance $\tfrac8{21}$. Given that, 7 of the 20 days left are losing. So the chance is $\tfrac{56}{420} = \tfrac2{15} \approx 0.1333$.

ideas: Condition by removing what you know and counting what is left: $\tfrac{25}{51}$ after one red.
Unseen cards change nothing: every position of a shuffled deck is alike.
$k$ special cards cut the other $n - k$ into $k + 1$ gaps of equal mean.

formula.name: First special card
formula.note: The first ace: $53/5 = 10.6$. The first heart: $53/14$.

summary.trap: Saying the card after the first ace is less likely to be the A♠. Building the decks shows it is exactly $\tfrac1{52}$.

quiz.prose: The first two cards dealt are both spades.
quiz.question: What is the chance the third card is a heart? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count hearts left over cards left.

byKey.ignore: You ignored the two spades dealt. Fewer cards are left, and no heart has gone.
byKey.den: You used 51 cards. Two have been dealt.

explain.text: No heart has gone, and 50 cards are left, so $13/50 = 0.26$.

quiz.prose: The first two cards dealt are both red.
quiz.question: What is the chance the bottom card of the deck is red? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: The bottom card is like any of the 50 unseen cards: $24/50 = 0.48$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Condition on the two red cards, then use symmetry for the rest.

byKey.half: You ignored the two red cards seen. Only 24 reds remain among 50.
byKey.one-gone: You removed one red card. Two have been seen.

explain.text: Given the two reds, the 50 unseen cards hold 24 reds. The bottom card is any of them alike. So the chance is $24/50 = 0.48$.

quiz.prose: Shuffle a deck and look only for the ace of spades.
quiz.question: On average, at what position is it? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: One special card makes two gaps: $(52 + 1)/2 = 26.5$.

byKey.half: You halved 52. Positions run from 1 to 52, so the middle is 26.5.

explain.text: With one special card the gap formula gives $53/2 = 26.5$, the average of 1 to 52. It is the edge case of $(n + 1)/(k + 1)$.

quiz.question: What is the chance the 10th card is the ace of hearts?

options.why: You removed nine cards nobody has seen. With no information, nothing is removed.
That is the chance the ace of hearts is somewhere in the first ten. The question names one place.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Nothing has been seen, so use symmetry.

explain.text: Unseen cards change nothing. The 10th card is any of the 52 with equal chance.
